item.title: Drift-invariant kernels for discount curve models
item.description: arXiv:2611.09751v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Kernel ridge regression estimates the discount curve as the minimizer of a pricing error plus a penalty given by the norm of a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. By the representer theorem, the estimate lies in a finite-dimensional affine space that depends only on the kernel and on the cash flow dates of the instruments. We ask when this space is invariant under the risk-neutral drift of the discount curve, so that the estimated curves can be the states of a continuous-time arbitrage-free model. We show that this holds for every grid of cash flow dates if and only if the kernel is of the form $k(x,y)=\e^{b(x+y)}\big(c\,\e^{axy}+1-c\big)$, apart from kernels whose Hilbert space has dimension at most two. For this kernel the estimated curve is an affine combination of flat discount curves, each corresponding to a constant continuously compounded yield. The drift-invariant subspaces correspond to sub-grids of the cash flow dates, and the discounted coefficients have linear risk-neutral dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Andreas Celary, Zehra Eksi-Altay, Damir Filipovic, Paul Kr\"uhner

item.title: The Long-Only Minimum Variance Portfolio in a One-Factor Market: Theory and Asymptotics
item.description: arXiv:2604.09986v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the long-only minimum variance (LOMV) portfolio, an object of interest going back to Markowitz, and the simplest non-trivial instance of quantitative portfolio construction. Despite its importance, aspects of the LOMV remain mysterious. Here we examine the base case of a general one-factor covariance model, and provide an explicit characterization of the solution. As a corollary we resolve an open question of Qi (2021) for this setting. In the high-dimensional regime of many assets, we prove that the active ratio (proportion of assets with non-zero weight in the LOMV portfolio) converges in almost all cases to a limit expressed in terms of the distribution of asset betas. In particular, when asset betas are all positive and drawn from a continuous distribution, the active ratio tends to zero in the high dimensional limit, and close to zero when the fraction of negative betas is small.
item.dc:creator: Alec Kercheval, Ololade Sowunmi
